prompt: What product forms when ethylene, H2C=CH2, is treated with HBr at room temperature?

choices.text: Bromoethane, CH3CH2Br
1,2-Dibromoethane, BrCH2CH2Br
choices.why: Only one Br is available per HBr. The H adds to one carbon and the Br to the other.

choices.text: Bromoethylene, H2C=CHBr, plus H2
choices.why: The double bond doesn't survive: its electrons are used to form the new C–H bond, so the product is saturated.

choices.text: Ethane, CH3CH3, plus Br2
choices.why: Both parts of HBr end up in the product; the reaction forms a C–H bond and a C–Br bond.

explanation: When ethylene is treated with HBr at room temperature, bromoethane is produced. H adds to one alkene carbon and Br to the other, an addition reaction.

prompt: What type of reaction is the addition of HBr to ethylene?

choices.text: A polar reaction known as an electrophilic addition
A radical substitution
choices.why: No radicals are involved, and nothing is replaced: electron pairs move from a nucleophile to an electrophile, and two reactants combine into one product.

choices.text: A polar elimination
choices.why: An elimination splits one reactant into two products. Here two reactants add together to give a single product.

choices.text: A nucleophilic addition, in which the alkene is attacked by an electron-rich reagent
choices.why: The alkene is itself the nucleophile; it is attacked by an electrophile, HBr. That is why the reaction is called an electrophilic addition.

explanation: The reaction is an example of a polar reaction type known as an electrophilic addition reaction: the electron-rich double bond reacts with the electrophile HBr, and the H and Br add to the two alkene carbons.

prompt: Why are alkanes such as ethane relatively inert?

choices.text: Their valence electrons are tied up in strong, nonpolar C–C and C–H bonds, sheltered in σ bonds between the nuclei
Their C–C bonds contain more electrons than a C=C bond
choices.why: It's the reverse: a single bond has two electrons, a double bond four. Alkanes are less electron-rich, not more.

choices.text: Their C–H bonds are strongly polar, so approaching reagents are repelled
choices.why: C–C and C–H bonds are nonpolar, so there is no electron-rich or electron-poor site to attract a reagent.

choices.text: Their bonding electrons lie above and below the plane of the molecule
choices.why: That describes π electrons, which are accessible. Alkane electrons are in σ bonds, between the nuclei.

explanation: Alkanes are relatively inert because all valence electrons are tied up in strong, nonpolar C–C and C–H bonds. The bonding electrons are also relatively inaccessible to approaching reactants because they are sheltered in σ bonds between nuclei.

prompt: How many electrons are in a carbon–carbon double bond?
explanation: Double bonds have a greater electron density than single bonds: four electrons in a double bond versus only two in a single bond. This is one reason the C=C bond is nucleophilic.

prompt: Why are the π electrons of a C=C bond more accessible to approaching reactants than σ electrons?

choices.text: They are located above and below the plane of the double bond rather than between the nuclei
The π bond is stronger than the σ bond
choices.why: The π bond is the weaker of the two (Figure 6.4.1). Accessibility comes from where the electrons are, not bond strength.

choices.text: The π electrons are held in sp^2 hybrid orbitals pointing directly at the reagent
choices.why: The sp^2–sp^2 overlap forms the σ part of the double bond. The π part comes from p–p overlap, above and below the plane.

choices.text: The π electrons carry a positive charge that attracts reagents
choices.why: Electrons are never positive. The double bond is the region of highest negative charge, which attracts electrophiles.

explanation: The electrons in the π bond are accessible to approaching reactants because they are located above and below the plane of the double bond rather than being sheltered between the nuclei (Figure 6.4.1).

prompt: In the C=C bond of ethylene, which orbital overlaps form the σ and π parts?

choices.text: σ from sp^2–sp^2 overlap; π from p–p overlap
σ from p–p overlap; π from sp^2–sp^2 overlap
choices.why: That is backward. Hybrid orbitals overlap head-on to make the σ bond; the unhybridized p orbitals overlap sideways to make the π bond.

choices.text: Both from sp^3–sp^3 overlap
choices.why: The alkene carbons are sp^2-hybridized, not sp^3, and a π bond can't come from hybrid orbitals.

choices.text: Both from sp^2–sp^2 overlap
choices.why: Only the σ part uses the sp^2 hybrids. The π part uses the p orbital left on each carbon.

explanation: A carbon–carbon double bond results from the orbital overlap of two sp^2-hybridized carbon atoms. The σ part results from sp^2–sp^2 overlap, and the π part results from p–p overlap (Section 1.8).

prompt: Compared with a carbon–carbon σ bond, how does a carbon–carbon π bond behave toward approaching reactants (Figure 6.4.1)?

choices.text: It is weaker, and its electrons are more accessible
It is stronger, and its electrons are more accessible
choices.why: The σ bond is the stronger one. The π bond is weaker, which, together with its accessibility, makes it reactive.

choices.text: It is stronger, and its electrons are less accessible
choices.why: That describes the σ bond: strong, with its electrons sheltered between the nuclei.

choices.text: It is weaker, and its electrons are less accessible
choices.why: The π electrons sit above and below the plane of the bond, so they are more accessible, not less.

explanation: Figure 6.4.1 compares the bonds: the σ bond is stronger, with less accessible bonding electrons; the π bond is weaker, with more accessible electrons. A double bond is both more accessible and more electron-rich (more nucleophilic) than a single bond.

prompt: In the reaction of ethylene with HBr, what role does the C=C double bond play?

choices.text: Nucleophile: it donates a pair of electrons
Electrophile: it accepts a pair of electrons
choices.why: The double bond is electron-rich, the region of highest negative charge. It gives electrons to HBr rather than taking them.

choices.text: Proton donor
choices.why: HBr is the proton donor. The alkene accepts the H^+ by using its π electrons to form a C–H bond.

choices.text: Radical: it donates one electron
choices.why: This is a polar reaction. The alkene donates a pair of electrons, not a single one.

explanation: Because a double bond is electron-rich and its π electrons are accessible, the double bond is nucleophilic, and the chemistry of alkenes is dominated by reactions with electrophiles. In the first step, the alkene donates a pair of electrons from its C=C bond to HBr.

prompt: Why does HBr act as the electrophile in its reaction with ethylene?

choices.text: As a strong acid, it is a powerful proton (H^+) donor
Its bromine has lone pairs it donates to the alkene
choices.why: Donating lone pairs would make HBr a nucleophile. The alkene donates electrons to the H of HBr.

choices.text: It is a weak acid that holds its proton tightly
choices.why: HBr is a strong acid; its readiness to give up H^+ is what makes it a powerful electrophile.

choices.text: It contains a C=C bond that accepts electrons
choices.why: HBr has no carbon at all. Its electrophilic site is the hydrogen.

explanation: As a strong acid, HBr is a powerful proton (H^+) donor and electrophile. The reaction between HBr and ethylene is therefore a typical electrophile–nucleophile combination, characteristic of all polar reactions.

prompt: In how many steps does the electrophilic addition of HBr to ethylene take place (Figure 6.4.2)?
explanation: The reaction takes place in two steps, both involving electrophile–nucleophile interactions: the alkene donates electrons to HBr to give a carbocation and Br^−, and then Br^− donates an electron pair to the carbocation (Figure 6.4.2).

prompt: In the first step of HBr addition to ethylene, where does the curved arrow that forms the new C–H bond start and end?

choices.text: It starts at the middle of the C=C bond and points to the H of HBr
It starts at the H of HBr and points to the C=C bond
choices.why: Curved arrows follow electrons, from the source of the pair to where the new bond forms. The electrons come from the double bond, not from H.

choices.text: It starts at the Br of HBr and points to a carbon
choices.why: The C–Br bond forms only in the second step, from Br^−. The first step forms the C–H bond.

choices.text: It starts at the middle of the C=C bond and points to the Br of HBr
choices.why: The new bond forms to hydrogen, so the arrow points to H. The H–Br electrons move onto Br with a separate arrow.

explanation: One curved arrow begins at the middle of the double bond (the source of the electron pair) and points to the hydrogen atom in HBr (the atom to which a bond will form). It shows that a new C–H bond forms using electrons from the former C=C bond.

prompt: In the first step of HBr addition to ethylene, a second curved arrow begins in the middle of the H–Br bond and points to Br. What does it show?

choices.text: The H–Br bond breaks and both electrons stay with Br, giving Br^−
The H–Br bond breaks and one electron goes to each atom
choices.why: That would give radicals. A curved arrow shows a pair moving, and both electrons go to the Br.

choices.text: Bromine donates a lone pair to form a new bond to hydrogen
choices.why: The arrow starts in the H–Br bond, so that bond is the one breaking; its electrons go onto Br.

choices.text: The H–Br bond breaks and the electrons stay with H, giving H^−
choices.why: The arrow points to Br, so the electrons end up on bromine; the H leaves as H^+ to bond with carbon.

explanation: Simultaneously with the C–H bond forming, a second curved arrow begins in the middle of the H–Br bond and points to the Br, indicating that the H–Br bond breaks and the electrons remain with the Br atom, giving Br^−.

prompt: After one alkene carbon of ethylene bonds to the incoming hydrogen, how many valence electrons does the other carbon have?
explanation: The other carbon has lost its share of the double-bond electrons, so it now has only six valence electrons and is left with a positive charge: a carbocation.

prompt: What role does the carbocation intermediate play in the second step of HBr addition to ethylene?

choices.text: It is an electrophile, accepting an electron pair from Br^−
It is a nucleophile, donating an electron pair to Br^−
choices.why: The carbocation carbon has only six valence electrons and a positive charge; it has room for a pair, not a pair to give.

choices.text: It is a radical, pairing its odd electron with one from bromine
choices.why: A carbocation has no unpaired electron. It accepts a whole pair from Br^− in a polar step.

choices.text: It donates H^+ to Br^− to regenerate HBr
choices.why: The observed product is bromoethane, formed when Br^− bonds to the positive carbon.

explanation: The carbocation is itself an electrophile that can accept an electron pair from the nucleophilic Br^− anion in a second step, forming a C–Br bond and yielding the observed addition product. A curved arrow shows the electron pair moving from Br^− to the positively charged carbon.

prompt: In the first step of HBr addition to ethylene, which carbon ends up with the positive charge?

choices.text: The carbon that did not bond to the hydrogen
The carbon that bonded to the hydrogen
choices.why: That carbon gained a new C–H bond and still has an octet. The other carbon lost its share of the double-bond electrons.

choices.text: Both carbons, each with half a positive charge
choices.why: The pair of π electrons goes into the C–H bond on one carbon, leaving the other carbon with six electrons and the whole charge.

choices.text: Neither; the positive charge stays on the hydrogen
choices.why: The hydrogen becomes part of a neutral C–H bond. The positive charge ends up on carbon, as a carbocation.

explanation: When one of the alkene carbons bonds to the incoming hydrogen, the other carbon, having lost its share of the double-bond electrons, has only six valence electrons and is left with a positive charge.

prompt: By analogy with ethylene, what product would you expect from the reaction of cyclopentene with HCl?

choices.text: Chlorocyclopentane
1,2-Dichlorocyclopentane
choices.why: One HCl supplies one H and one Cl, so only one chlorine is added, with H on the other alkene carbon.

choices.text: Cyclopentane
choices.why: That would be adding H to both carbons. The second step bonds Cl^− to the carbocation.

choices.text: Chlorocyclopentene
choices.why: The C=C bond's electrons are used to form the new C–H bond, so the double bond is gone in the product.

explanation: Like ethylene with HBr, the alkene's C=C bond donates an electron pair to H of HCl, giving a carbocation and Cl^−; Cl^− then bonds to the positive carbon. H and Cl add across the former double bond, giving chlorocyclopentane.

prompt: What do all polar reactions have in common?

choices.text: They take place between an electron-poor site and an electron-rich site, with an electron pair donated from a nucleophile to an electrophile
They all involve an alkene and HBr
choices.why: HBr addition to ethylene is only one example of a polar process; there are many others.

choices.text: Each bonding electron pair splits, one electron going to each atom
choices.why: That is how radicals form. In polar reactions electrons move in pairs.

choices.text: An electrophile donates an electron pair to a nucleophile
choices.why: The direction is backward: the nucleophile is the electron-rich donor and the electrophile the acceptor.

explanation: Regardless of the details of individual reactions, all polar reactions take place between an electron-poor site and an electron-rich site and involve the donation of an electron pair from a nucleophile to an electrophile.
